Listen to our selected series of podcast episodes by @museumofblackfutures — a mobile art and heritage laboratory that works with communities, artists, and thinkers to imagine new forms of cultural infrastructure rooted in Black joy, radical imagination, and spiritual reparations.⁠
⁠
In this episode Lelani Lewis and podcast host Richard Kofi reflect on what it means to return not only cultural objects, but also the practices, ingredients, and traditions shaped by displacement and colonial histories. Together, they trace food as archive, ceremony, and a living connection to memory, community, and belonging. @richardkofiart @lelani_lewis @atelier_code_noir⁠

Already working on the African continent or planning to? ⁠

Join re:publica x Contemporary And (C&) on May 18 at STATION Berlin, to meet stakeholders shaping art, creative industries, tech and knowledge across Africa and its Global Diaspora. With Yvette Mutumba, Chloë Sylvestre and Olivia Buschey.

⁠
We begin by resurfacing this text from the C& archive, in which Eric Otieno Sumba reflects on the 59th Venice Biennale, arguing that the event's brand of worldliness is, at its core, a form of provincialism.⁠

Ndidi Dike speaks with C& about her exhibition "Rare Earth Rare Justice", unpacking how resource extraction is linked to global systems of violence. Through sound, colour, and material, she connects mining, infrastructure, and the ongoing exploitation of land and labour, reflecting on how these histories are carried in the materials she uses. @ndidi.dike⁠

Khanyisile Mbongwa joins @amoskonst as Curator of Art in the Public Realm.⁠
⁠
Curatorial theorist, sociologist, and Sangoma, @ebuhlanti_republik approaches curating as an ethical, political, and spiritual practice that connects contemporary art with ancestral knowledge and emancipatory imaginaries.⁠
⁠
She previously curated the 12th Liverpool Biennial and is the founding curator of the Stellenbosch Triennale. Her research engages with the human condition, Black Radical Traditions, Trans-Indigeneity, BIPOC-queer aesthetics, and ways of imagining alternative futures through black lived experiences and ancestral knowledges. ⁠

How do we listen to the ocean?⁠
In "Sounding the Ocean: Spiral Networks of Remembrance and Elation", Dr. Hiba Ali reflects on ocean-sensing as an immersive, somatic, and durational practice of listening. 

The piece brings together performance text, images, and moving visuals from the work, alongside a short story presented in English and in a Swahili translation.⁠

Nigerian-American artist Zainab Aliyu’s @beatsbyzai exhibition ‘A litany for past suns’ brings together stereographic images, installation, text and sculpture. Drawing on personal and community archives, the exhibition reflects on how systems of knowledge and classification are shaped by colonial histories.⁠
⁠
Positioned among a lineage of Black feminist archival critique, A litany for past suns draws from scholars such as Safiya Noble, Tina Campt, and Saidiya Hartman, who articulate the tensions between machine logic and ancestral memory.⁠
⁠
On view @baxterstccny in New York through April 2, 2026.⁠
⁠
For more info follow link in bio!⁠

⁠
For more than two decades, Muholi’s work has powerfully centred and celebrated Black LGBTQIA+ communities through portraiture and visual activism, reshaping conversations around representation, identity, and human rights.⁠
⁠
The award includes SEK 2,000,000, a gold medal and a camera, with a major solo exhibition opening at the Hasselblad Center in Gothenburg in October 2026. @hasselbladfoundation

To mark a pivotal transition as we settle into the year, C& Magazine’s editorial team reflects on ideas of continuities and discontinuities within our approach.⁠
⁠
Citing inspiration from methodologies such as counterpointed repetition, a poetic technique by Marlene Nourbese Philip used to deconstruct, disrupt, and re-narrate an archive, newly appointed C& Managing Editor Naima Hassan, alongside C& Editor-in-Chief Ethel-Ruth Tawe, engage with key episodes from the magazine’s 13-year history. 'Notes on Editorial Dis/Continuities' reflects on questions of stewardship and gestures through which those who came before are honoured.⁠
⁠
A limited number of print copies are available for pick-up at the C& Berlin and Nairobi offices. Please enquire by emailing info@contemporaryand.com with the subject line: pamphlet.⁠

Read the digital version of the pamphlet via Link in Bio⁠

The 13th edition of Investec Cape Town Art Fair concluded this weekend, and C& joined as an official media partner.⁠
⁠
From 20–22 February 2026, the fair brought together exhibitors and artists across geographies and generations, the fair unfolds under the curatorial proposition "Listen", inviting audiences to reflect on sound, silence, resonance, and resistance, as it asks how art can shift the ways we hear, see, and think.⁠
⁠
As part of the talks programme, C& Editor-in-Chief Ethel-Ruth Tawe participated in ‘Africa is a Country: Unpacking Tensions between Unity and Difference’, a conversation that embraces the literary phrase as both critique and possibility. ⁠
A tribute to Koyo Kouoh’s curatorial legacy and her insistence on rigour and epistemic freedom, the discussion reflects on Pan-Africanism rooted in solidarity rather than sameness.⁠
⁠
Find out more about the fair — and its all-female team — via 👉@investeccapetownartfair⁠

From Manet’s Olympia to Hollywood’s Oscars, Stephanie Tinsley traces a recurring pattern she names the "Olympia Effect". By moving between western art history, contemporary film and pop culture, she shows how narratives of sex, agency, and desire are repeatedly legitimised only once they are centred on a white protagonist.⁠
⁠
Across contemporary culture – from Zola to Christina Aguilera’s Stripped – the same logic persists: Black femininity signals rebellion and modernity, while Black women are denied authorship, humanity, and reward.⁠
⁠
Read the full opinion piece via link in bio and join the discussion!

DADDY announces THE LAND REMEMBERS, a new exhibition inviting artists to submit visual works engaging with Waste Colonialism. The show examines how excess consumption and plastic waste from the Global North are displaced to the Global South, revealing an uneven system masked by narratives of donation, sustainability, and so called “eye level” exchange.⁠
⁠
Artists are invited to question how land, water, and bodies carry the traces of what the world tries to forget.⁠

In an audiovisual response to an archive at the Warburg Institute, Edward George traces how images of Blackness move through time. In conversation with writer Yaa Addae, he reflects on recurring visual motifs, the weight of the archive, and what it means to look with intention. @yaa.dae⁠

YATTA’s Iron + Palm Wine is now on View @art_omi

“Iron + Palm Wine” connects West African guitar history with today’s listening and the rhythms of nature, drawing on the legacy of palm wine music and the stories it carries. The show is spiritually rooted in the music of S. E. Rogie, the renowned Sierra Leonean guitarist and a pioneer of palm wine music. Through video, sound, and intimate interviews, @yatta.sound opens up a space for conversation around Black wandering, reflecting on land, history, and freedom. 

The exhibition is on view until February 2 in New York.

Pélagie Gbaguidi and her Poetics of Memory⁠

Her paintings and drawings activate the gaps of history—what’s been omitted, silenced, or erased—turning them into spaces of resistance and reflection. Through layers of color, gesture, and fragment, she challenges how we see and remember, addressing the viewer through what is hidden or repressed in dominant narratives.⁠

The Art of Dialogue: Living Archives, Memory and Practice⁠
⁠
At this year’s @fnbartjoburg, C& curated an intergenerational exchange between artist Sam Nhlengethwa, writer Gillian Fleischmann, and C& Director Yvette Mutumba to explore archives, memory, and artistic practice.⁠
@sam.nhlengethwa @gillian_f_⁠
⁠
Reflecting on the conversation, Fleischmann argues that intergenerational exchange is like a living collage—a generative site of transition. Archives, too, are living spaces shaped by people, but often limited by institutions.⁠
How can we dismantle decades of systemic convention, spark intergenerational exchange, and open archives to wider engagement?⁠

Caribbean Abstraction: Persistent Color by Kenwyn Crichlow⁠
⁠
Citizen Projects joins @theatlantaartweek to present the first Atlanta solo exhibition of Trinidadian painter, arts leader, and educator Kenwyn Crichlow.⁠
⁠
Large-scale and gestural, Crichlow’s abstract works are shaped by Trinidad’s topography and natural light, created in his Curepe studio where shadows and creeping vines inspire his color theory. ⁠
⁠
Founded in 2022 by Aida Esi Hayfron-Benjamin in Accra, @citizenprojectspace has grown from an independent curatorial practice into a gallery space dedicated to slow, thoughtful collaborations connecting the Caribbean, Africa, and the African American diaspora.⁠
⁠
The exhibition will be on view in Atlanta from Oct 3- 11, 2025!⁠

The Ciccillo Matarazzo Pavilion opens its doors to the 36th Bienal de São Paulo with an exhibition featuring more than 120 artists who shape an experience that goes beyond the visual, appealing to a multisensory sensibility. The tour is not imposed; it reveals itself slowly, amid underground sounds emanating from the bowels of the building, making the visitor’s body vibrate to the rhythm of their footsteps between floors.

Curated by Bonaventure Soh Bejeng Ndikung and his team, the exhibition is conceived as a poetics of care. Art is summoned as a medium for healing, rethinking, and regenerating what it means to be human. The title: Calma e do silêncio, taken from a poem by Afro-Brazilian writer Conceição Evaristo—is not only evocative, but also programmatic.

The exhibition unfolds along three major curatorial axes, articulated through six interconnected chapters that flow like tributaries into a shared estuary. Far from being a decorative metaphor, the image of the estuary underpins the entire experience: different currents of thought, history, spirituality converge, clash, and coexist. The curatorial narrative eschews linear explanation in favor of a symbolic and atmospheric language, one that speaks more to the senses than to reason. At times, however, this museographic structure breaks its own current, leaving us stranded in a desolate ultramarine.

The Biennal begins with a garden created by Precious Okoyomon, which transforms the pavilion into a living geography with plants from the Cerrado, the Caribbean, and the Americas, evoking memories of migration and colonial violence. Poetry guides the experience like an emotional compass.

Works such as Unearthed – Sunlight by Otobong Nkanga reflect on the interdependence between humans and nature, while Portals to Submerged Worlds by Moffat Takadiwa transforms waste into sacred architecture, proposing sustainable futures.

The Biennial raises questions and creates fruitful tensions between different worlds. Through poetry and silence, it invites us to imagine other paths where art is a practice of listening, paying attention, and being radically open to others.

Horace Pippin: From soldier to painter⁠
⁠
After fighting in WWI with the Harlem Hellfighters and surviving a sniper’s bullet to his right arm, Horace Pippin (1888–1946) turned to painting as a way to heal. What began as therapy became his life’s work.⁠
⁠
In "Old Black Joe", Pippin shows an old Black man tied to a white boy, set against the backdrop of a cotton field. The title refers to an 1860s ballad that romanticized slavery and saw a revival around 1940. Pippin’s painting directly challenges this nostalgic view by revealing the harsh, enduring realities behind the song. His subject remains bound, both physically and spiritually, to a painful past that offers no comfort and no release.⁠

The @whitneymuseum presents the eighty-first edition of the Whitney Biennial, the longest-running contemporary art exhibition in the United States, featuring seventy-one artists and two collectives that address many of today's pressing issues. With this exhibition we are committed to amplifying the voices of artists who confront these legacies and to providing a space where difficult ideas can be addressed and considered.⁠
⁠
This Biennial brings together artists who explore the permeability of mind-body relationships, the fluidity of identity, and the increasing precariousness of the natural and constructed worlds around us. Whether through subversive humor, expressive abstraction, or non-Western forms of cosmological thought, to name a few of their methods, these artists demonstrate that there are still paths to be found, strategies to be discovered for coping and healing, and ways to come together even in a fractured age.⁠

Dear arts workers all around the world, we need to clarify something about the 2024 Dak’Art Biennial.⁠

The OFF is ON! But this message is like a broken record. It fails to capture who’s calling the shots (IN) and who’s pushing boundaries underground (OFF). Let’s cut through the noise. And the biennial is their masterpiece.⁠
⁠
The Dakar Biennale is a mixtape with the Ministry of Culture taking center stage. But the beat of Dakar? It’s in the streets, the hidden galleries, the spontaneous performances. Despite the ministry’s influence, Dakar’s artists hold the rhythm. The biennial’s postponement? That’s bureaucratic red tape stifling the cultural rhythm. The biennial is part of Dakar’s cultural fabric—let’s amplify the voices of the underground. When the biennial hits pause—that’s the Ministry of Culture’s playlist, not the sound of Dakar’s creative pulse. The OFF scene? It’s electric. It sets trends while the establishment plays catch-up.⁠

Venice Biennale: Miles Greenberg

The artist Miles Greenberg presented the performance piece (SEBASTIAN, 2024) at the Berggruen Museum - Neue Nationalgalerie, jointly curated by Klaus Biesenbach and Lisa Botti. In a durational format, the artist appears on a Lido stone on a rotating platform, pierced by five arrows. Greenberg unites different worlds, referencing religious references such as the saint and martyr Saint Sebastian and the avant-garde of technology, as he is surrounded by four cameras that follow his movements and perform a 3D scan of his body. With a dispossessed look, the artist’s black makeup is washed away by syrup falling from the ceiling of the enclosure.

This performance connects with the representation of the Martyr Saint Sebastian, in II Sodoma (around 1525). Condemned to die by Emperor Maximian for professing his religion, arrows pierced his body but failed to take his life. It was flogging by the military that accomplished the mission.

Greenberg connects to the historic motifs of the Venetian black chamois by Andrea Brustolon with an unauthorized 3D reproduction of Brustolon’s carved concolle for vases (Ca’ Rezzonico, Venice).

The artist rethinks the European canon through these recurring characters from various mythologies, and explores how it can respond to this exercise of representing religious and mythological figures that has been repeated throughout the history of Western art. In addition, Greenberg reviews the representation of black motifs in architecture, in this case in Venice and  discusses how these motifs are omnipresent yet anonymous and nameless, despite their constant presence.

Venice Biennial: US Pavilion⁠
⁠
An example of the mobilization of critical and decolonial thinking emerged outside the US pavilion, represented by Mississippi-born Choctaw/Cherokee American artist Jeffrey Gibson, who was accompanied by intertribal Native American dancers and singers from Oklahoma and Colorado, who came to Venice to blaze a historic trail.⁠
@jeffrune⁠
@labiennale⁠
⁠
Located in Giardini, this pavilion is presented with a chromatic range of many colors, a large red sculpture composed of pedestals of different heights that already told us that it would be the stage to expose the message of the artist project of the U.S. pavilion, but that was also the scene of protests and peaceful demonstrations that manifest the commitment of art and artists with the most sensitive political issues such as the genocide of the people of Palestine.⁠
⁠
The pavilion with the title: "The space in which to place me" invites us to review the political history of the United States, the erasure of native peoples and the civil responsibility of this country with the native peoples, who still persist in maintaining their traditions.⁠
⁠
Between installations, banners, videos, handcrafted sculptures, paintings with geometric motifs and evocative texts, they are the explosive dose of color and political references to Native American and American history. The artist's work is a tribute to the family lineage, denouncing the violence that even his own parents experienced.⁠
⁠
In one work we read a text that is part of a real letter from 1902 written by the Commissioner of Indian Affairs to a school superintendent: "The returned male student far too frequently goes back to the reservation and falls into the old custom of letting his hair grow long" Gibson presents us with busts with prominent hair; long and loose locks made with tape. These are some of the gestures that he critically rewrites.⁠

How Jacolby Satterwhite is redefining art through virtual reality and beyond⁠

Jacolby Satterwhite is renowned for a conceptual practice that addresses crucial themes of labor, consumption, carnality and fantasy through immersive installations, virtual reality and digital media. He uses a variety of software to produce intricately detailed animations and live action films of real and imaginary worlds populated by avatars of artists and friends. An equally significant influence is that of his late mother, Patricia Satterwhite, whose ethereal voices and diagrams of visionary household products serve as source material within a decidedly complex structure of memory and mythology.⁠

Stranieri Ovunque/Foreigners Everywhere - Venice Biennale

The 60th International Art Exhibition in Venice promises a powerful exploration of identity and belonging in a complex world. Curated by Adriano Pedrosa, "Foreigners Everywhere" takes its name from a Turin-based collective that fought against racism and xenophobia in Italy in the early 2000s: Stranieri Ovunque.

Adriano Pedrosa explains: "The background of the work is a world plagued by multiple crises related to the movement and existence of people across countries, nations, territories and borders, reflecting the dangers and pitfalls of language, translation and ethnicity, expressing differences and disparities conditioned by identity, nationality, race, gender, sexuality, wealth and freedom. In this landscape, the phrase Foreigners Everywhere has (at least) a double meaning. First, that wherever you go and wherever you are, you will always find foreigners: they/we are everywhere. Secondly, that no matter where you are, you are always, really and truly, a foreigner."
